item.title: The Road Down to Westfall
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Andric stood in the Valley of Heroes again that evening, under the stone kings, close enough to the Cathedral to hear its bells. He didn’t go up the steps this time. He turned around and walked back out through the gate. The chronicle records the visit. It doesn’t record what he came for, or what made him leave.
item.content:encoded:
Andric stood in the Valley of Heroes again that evening, under the stone kings, close enough to the Cathedral to hear its bells. He didn’t go up the steps this time. He turned around and walked back out through the gate. The chronicle records the visit. It doesn’t record what he came for, or what made him leave.

What it records next is the road. Down from Goldshire, past the last farms of Elwynn, to the place where the forest just stops. The trees thin, the fences start leaning, and the ground goes the color of old straw. That’s Westfall. It was the breadbasket of Stormwind once. Now it’s mostly wind.

Just past the Jansen Stead, a broken wagon sat by the road with an old couple beside it. Farmer Furlbrow and his wife Verna had packed what they could carry and run in the night. Their fields were full of hooligans, Furlbrow said. In his rush he’d left his pocket watch in the farmhouse wardrobe, the one Verna’s father gave him on their wedding day. Verna’s horse, Poor Old Blanchy, needed oats from fields that weren’t safe to walk anymore. And Verna wanted her recipe for Westfall stew carried to Salma Saldean down the road, because a woman leaving her home for good wants to leave something behind.

Andric said yes to all three. Of course he did.

Here is what the chronicler knows, and Andric knows it better. The men in Furlbrow’s fields wear red bandanas and call themselves the Defias. Before that they were the Stonemasons Guild, the men who rebuilt Stormwind and never got paid for it. Some of them, years ago, lay in an Old Town cellar with broken ribs while a young acolyte from the Cathedral sat up with them through the night. Some of their sons may be in those fields now.

Furlbrow called them thieves. He isn’t wrong. They stole his farm. The Cathedral called them traitors, and Andric once asked where that was written. Out here, with the wind coming over the wheat and an old horse looking at him, nobody’s going to ask him what he thinks the Light says about it. They’ll just want to know whose side he’s on.

Gryan Stoutmantle’s letter is still in his satchel, unopened. Sentinel Hill is a few miles south. The pumpkin farm is right over the rise.

item.title: Rip Willink: The Man Who Walked Into Northshire
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Nobody in Elwynn knew where Rip Willink came from. He walked up the road into Northshire Valley one gray afternoon with no horse, no pack and no friends. He had long black hair, a plain blade on his hip, a sealed letter in his vest and the patient look of a man who has already counted the exits.
item.content:encoded:
Nobody in Elwynn knew where Rip Willink came from. He walked up the road into Northshire Valley one gray afternoon with no horse, no pack and no friends. He had long black hair, a plain blade on his hip, a sealed letter in his vest and the patient look of a man who has already counted the exits.

He’d been a soldier once, in some company that no longer existed after a war that got no songs. He didn’t talk about it. He carried one rule instead of a past: if you see something wrong and you can fix it, you fix it.

Northshire Abbey has been taking in volunteers for as long as Stormwind has had troubles it can’t spare the men for. Deputy Willem was waiting in the valley the way he always is, with his belt already tightened and a finger pointed at the abbey door. A Threat Within, he called it. Rip went in and reported to Marshal McBride. McBride looked at him the way he looks at every volunteer these days, like a man hoping there would be enough of them and not at all sure there would be.

McBride sent him north, where a clan of kobolds had infested the woods. Outside, Eagan Peltskinner had a simpler arrangement. He hates the timber wolves and likes wolf steaks, and he’ll trade something useful for eight pieces of tough wolf meat.

Rip learned to skin first. Then, out among the young wolves, a column of gold light rose out of the valley and left him a little harder to kill. The blade felt the same.

He went into the kobolds after that. One of them dropped a book that looked like the kobold had tried to eat it. It had to have come from Brother Paxton’s little library inside the abbey. Rip took the errand. He didn’t take the book back. Not yet.

He also learned to mine and to smelt copper, which is a lot of trade for a man who hadn’t finished his first two jobs or returned a half-eaten book to a librarian. That first day was short. He earned forty-one copper, spent thirty, and left the valley for the night with two quests done, three still open and a nibbled book in his pack.

He came back the next day around midday, and the valley picked up where it had left off.

The light found him again almost at once, out in the grass below the abbey. Deputy Willem had a new grievance waiting. The Defias had crept into Northshire itself, thugs in red burlap bandanas loitering by the vineyards, and Willem wanted the bandanas brought back as proof. Rip took the job. Men who think nobody will stop them were exactly his kind of problem.

Then there was the letter. It had ridden with him all the way up the road, addressed to a man in the abbey the brothers don’t talk about much. Jorik Kerridan keeps to a dim loft above the main hall, in a striped shirt, with the easy smile of a man who has already counted your pockets. “You look like the type I should watch my coin purse around,” he said, which from Jorik is a compliment. He read the letter and taught Rip the first thing every one of his kind has to know: how to stand in a room and not be there.

The book finally went home. Brother Paxton turned it over in his hands like a man reading his own obituary and sent Rip to his assistant, Daniel, to count what else was gone. Daniel had warned Paxton three times about the kobolds tunneling under the abbey, and whole shelves were empty. Paxton wanted eight of his books back before the kobolds ate the rest of the library. Eagan Peltskinner finally got his wolf meat.

So Rip went down into Echo Ridge Mine, among the candle-headed kobolds, their carts and their stolen reading. Somewhere in the timbered dark, the gold light came a third time. When it faded, a kobold the size of a small man, Shinyfinder Narf, lay still in the dust beside him, and the laborers were backing away. The chronicle records the body. It doesn’t record a scratch on the rogue.

He climbed out with Paxton’s eight books under his arm, and Jorik taught him two more lessons the abbey would rather not hear about: where to put a blade in a man who isn’t looking, and how to lift a purse from one who is.

The road out of Northshire runs down to Goldshire, and the next morning so did Rip. He cleared out the Fargodeep Mine for a while alongside a stranger named Oljoel, and the abbey got the last of its books back. He paid for his lessons at the Lion’s Pride Inn, learning how to slip a blow and how to finish a man who’s already reeling, then hauled a shipment of kobold candles all the way to Stormwind’s Trade District, because somebody had to.

Elwynn kept handing him small troubles, and he kept fixing them. He found Billy Maclure’s lost necklace and bought him a pie, and he carried a note between two young lovers whose families didn’t approve. He helped a murloc-hunted farmhand named Maybell make her escape, and he tried his hand at fishing at Crystal Lake. He walked the halls of the Tower of Azora and went down Jasperlode Mine with a man named Darlan. By the time he reached the water at Jerod’s Landing, he was a good deal harder to kill than the man who’d come up the road.

Back at the Lion’s Pride, he bought one meal, paid in exact copper and sat with his back to the wall. That was the night three Defias toughs came in to collect their “road tax” from the innkeeper. Rip watched them for a while, finished his stew and stood up.

The fight lasted about as long as it takes to tell. He didn’t use the blade. When it was over, he set the innkeeper’s chair back upright, left an extra copper for the broken mug and sat back down.

A quiet woman in the corner had watched the whole thing. She didn’t give a name, only the SI:7 seal, and a direction: Old Town, Stormwind. There, Master Mathias Shaw laid out the job. The Defias were running contraband through Jerod’s Landing, and he needed the dockmaster’s shipping schedule.

“I don’t work for anybody,” Rip said.

“You don’t have to,” said Shaw. “Just get it.”

The first time, the dock house won. Somebody saw him, the fight went wrong, and Rip Willink died face down on the planks at Jerod’s Landing. SI:7, true to its word, knew nothing about it.

He came back anyway. The second time he did it right. He slipped in after dark, lifted the schedule straight out of the goblin’s pocket and was gone before anyone missed it. Shaw read it, looked at him for a long moment and handed him a blade.

“SI:7 will disavow all knowledge of you,” Shaw said.

“Good,” said Rip. “I’d hate to be on somebody’s list.”

Then came a delivery that sent him far from home. He rode the Deeprun Tram under the mountains to Ironforge, walked through the snows of Dun Morogh and the North Gate Pass, and came down into Loch Modan. At Algaz Station he handed Stormpike’s delivery to the dwarves holding the pass and took their order back. He had a look at Thelsamar, then headed home to Stormwind.

That afternoon he found Westbrook Garrison begging for help. There was a bounty on Riverpaw gnolls and a wanted poster with a name every Elwynn farmer knows: Hogger. Rip ran the gnoll hills with a fighter named Kolebalt, and by evening the bounty was paid. The Hogger poster came down for good, and the gold light found him a fourth time on the streets of Goldshire.

He wasn’t finished. The guards in Eastvale had gone missing, and someone had made off with a shopkeeper’s enchanting supplies. There was steel to fetch and linen to deliver. He walked out past the Eastvale Logging Camp and down to Stone Cairn Lake with a fresh list of other people’s problems.

He finished Elwynn the way he’d started it, one small trouble at a time. The lost guards of Eastvale turned up, and so did Rolf, by a murloc camp on Stone Cairn Lake, past anybody’s help. Rip carried Guard Thomas’s report down to Marshal Dughan in Goldshire. Hamish Bergwort got his delicate instruments working again, the enchanting supplies went back where they belonged, and the gold light found him once more on the road. Princess, the prize sow of Brackwell Pumpkin Patch, found the end of her story. Then he took the road west.

Westfall begins where the trees give up. Past the Jansen Stead, Farmer Furlbrow and his wife Verna sat beside a broken wagon with everything they still owned, and an old horse named Blanchy too tired to pull it. The fields were full of thieves, Verna said, and worse, machines. Furlbrow had left his pocket watch in the farmhouse wardrobe, the one Verna’s father gave him on their wedding day.

Rip went to get it. Furlbrow’s Pumpkin Farm killed him twice for the trouble. The third time he came back with the watch and a few handfuls of oats, and an old horse ate well that morning. The gold light caught him again among the Furlbrows’ wheat.

Verna sent him on to Salma Saldean with her stew recipe, and Salma, who knows a strong back when she sees one, found more work for it. At Sentinel Hill, Gryan Stoutmantle was raising the People’s Militia out of farmers with nothing left to lose. Gryan wanted Defias trappers and smugglers dead. Scout Galiaan wanted red leather bandanas, the kind the gang wear. Quartermaster Lewis wanted a note carried to Old Town and put Rip on a gryphon to get it there faster.

Then Longshore, where the murlocs keep the coast. The chronicler stopped counting the men who die on Westfall’s sand a long time ago. Rip died there four times over two days. He kept coming back.

The next morning he found company. A mage named Muddo fell in with him, and Darksides, Tammy, Imp and Much drifted in and out of the party, the way strangers do on a road nobody likes to walk alone. By the time Muddo went his own way, Rip had his bandanas. Galiaan paid, Gryan counted the dead and nodded, and the gold light found Rip again at the foot of Sentinel Tower.

Gryan had another job ready, the kind that comes with a name. The Defias Brotherhood, he called it, and the trail runs east to a man called Wiley the Black, upstairs at the inn in Lakeshire. Rip went to Old Town first, to the men who taught him his trade, and learned how to take a man from behind without a sound. Then he went back to Westfall.

There are fewer Defias bandanas in Westfall now. Somewhere past it, the rest of the Brotherhood is about to find out he meant it.

item.title: Orders for Bethor Iceshard
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: “Either you do not know who I am, or your business with me is urgent.”
item.content:encoded:
“Either you do not know who I am, or your business with me is urgent.”

Bethor Iceshard said it without looking up, in the purple gloom of the Undercity’s Magic Quarter, where the canals run green and nobody has breathed in years. Ghoulsbie held out Magistrate Sevren’s orders. They had been in his pack since Brill, through the gnolls and the murlocs and the keep on the bluffs and one death the chronicle still cannot explain. Bethor read them. “Ah, you are the agent sent by Magistrate Sevren. Then yes, your business with me is crucial.” A pause, of the kind mages keep in stock. “I trust Sevren has mustered someone suitable for my task. But we shall see.”

The chronicler has seen that look given to a great many adventurers. It is the look a man gives a shovel before he finds out whether it will break.

The morning had started stranger. Ghoulsbie woke in the Canals, where he had last lain down, and for the space of a breath he was not on the rolls of the Goblin News Network. Then he was again, at the same rank as before: Corporate Asset. The dead do not get promoted, it seems. They do not get let go either.

Bethor’s task, when it came, was a theft dressed up as recruitment. There is a lich on the island in Brightwater Lake, north of the city. He is Forsaken, free-willed, his own master, and he is convinced that every other undead thing in Tirisfal is still a slave of the Scourge. So he sets his minions on anyone who comes near. The Queen will want him anyway, Bethor said, and if he is any good at necromancy, his knowledge would be quite useful. Nobody knows his name. Ghoulsbie is to slip into his camp, steal his spellbook and bring it back, so Bethor can find out who he was.

The chronicler would point out, if anyone asked, that this lich believes about every other Forsaken roughly what Danitha Morr’s own people believe about her risen paladins: that whatever stands up out of a grave is still owned by someone. The lich may even be half right. Ghoulsbie carries the Light, and an Undercity mage’s errand, and a goblin company’s title, and he has not yet said which of them he answers to.

He did not go to the lake. Not yet. He climbed up out of the Undercity instead, into the Ruins of Lordaeron, the broken throne city his first life served, and stopped there under the open sky with the book still unstolen. The lich is still on his island. He does not know that anyone is coming. He would not believe it was anyone free.

item.title: The Cathedral Sends for Its Novice
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The stained glass of the Cathedral of Light throws its colors on the floor the same way it did the day they sent him away. Andric stood in them anyway. High Priestess Laurena was waiting by the lectern, between the candles, and she said the thing the Cathedral says to everyone it has decided to keep: “I’m glad you’ve arrived. There are many things we will have to discuss, but more importantly is your training in the ways of the Light.”
item.content:encoded:
The stained glass of the Cathedral of Light throws its colors on the floor the same way it did the day they sent him away. Andric stood in them anyway. High Priestess Laurena was waiting by the lectern, between the candles, and she said the thing the Cathedral says to everyone it has decided to keep: “I’m glad you’ve arrived. There are many things we will have to discuss, but more importantly is your training in the ways of the Light.”

Many things to discuss. The chronicler noticed that she did not discuss them.

The summons had come by way of Priestess Josetta, upstairs at the Lion’s Pride Inn, and it had been riding in his satchel for days with a murloc’s head and an unopened decision. You’ve caught the attention of our superiors, it said. Apparently they feel you’ve proven yourself already. The same superiors, presumably, who once moved him to Northshire for bandaging masons in the Old Town cellars. Andric had walked as far as the Valley of Heroes before, and turned back. This time he went up the steps. He came out with a new prayer, Divine Grace, and no apology, which is the usual exchange rate.

He had earned the walk, if anyone earns anything in Elwynn. The day began on the Stonefield farm and ended the Stonefield and Maclure business, or as much of it as one priest can end. Princess, the prize sow of Brackwell Pumpkin Patch, is no more, and Ma Stonefield has her brass collar. Goldtooth’s stolen necklace went home to Auntie Bernice. And the little bottle William Pestle poured, the one Andric had carried so long he might have been trying to decide whether to drink it himself, went at last to Maybell Maclure. She drank it, and her family will not see her go to Tommy Joe Stonefield. Andric decided it was a kindness. The chronicler hopes he is right. Families who will not share a fence rarely forgive the man who helped one of them climb it.

Then Jerod’s Landing, and the murlocs, who forgive nothing. Andric died there twice around midday and twice more that afternoon, face-down at the water’s edge. A stranger named Luky stood by him for a moment between deaths and moved on. On one of the long walks back he strayed again over the Darkened Bank into Duskwood, and came straight back out again, a man who has learned which doors to leave shut. In the end Guard Thomas had his eight fins. Sara Timberlain at the logging camp had her red linen bandanas off Defias necks, and the chronicler will not repeat what he wrote last time about whose sons wear them. Andric did not say it either. And Croaky’s head went at last to Merell Ross, the watch captain at Ridgepoint Tower, on the high road toward Redridge, where the wind smells of other people’s wars.

After the Cathedral, the work came faster, the way it does when a man has stopped arguing with himself. Back at the inn the camping teacher showed him how to make a proper first aid kit, which is more than the Cathedral ever taught him about the wounded. At the Tower of Azora, Hamish Bergwort complained that the kobolds’ crude magic kept throwing off his delicate instruments, so Andric went into the Jasperlode Mine and thinned the Kobold Geomancers, and a passer-by named Apollo walked with him for a few minutes that evening. Hamish wanted more, and got it. Hagar Lowe got his good steel, mining tools fished out of kobold buckets. Blixie Fitzwink, the apprentice who dropped Master Theocritus’s enchanting supplies when the gnolls sprang an ambush, got them back from the camps above Stone Cairn Lake and was spared weeks of cleaning up after polymorph experiments. Marshal Dughan got his report on the mine. Brother Paxton, up at the abbey where all of this began, got the last two books of his stolen library, pried from a kobold geosculptor named Yip and a spider called Mother Fang. Somewhere in there Andric grew stronger, and Josetta gave him the Inner Fire, a light worn like armor.

Then west, to Westbrook Garrison, where Deputy Rainer was short of everything except gnolls. A traveller named Rhope fell in beside him for a moment and went their own way. The Riverpaw lost a great many painted armbands. And by full dark, Andric stood in the lamplight of Goldshire and put a huge gnoll claw into Marshal Dughan’s hand.

Hogger’s.

Every child in Elwynn grows up afraid of Hogger, and every novice who survives the forest ends up chasing him. The chronicle does not say how the big gnoll fell, or who stood with Andric when he did. It records the claw, the marshal’s nod, and a priest who healed for a living walking away into the dark with blood under his nails.

Sixty-odd silver earned that day, twenty-odd spent. Elwynn is nearly finished with him. The letter for Gryan Stoutmantle at Sentinel Hill is still in the satchel, and Westfall is where the masons’ sons went. And somewhere under the stained glass, High Priestess Laurena has many things to discuss with him. She has not said what they are. He has not asked.

item.title: Guests in the Windlord’s Realm
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: “Enjoy your remaining time as ‘guests’ in my lord’s realm,” said Rohash, Lord of the East Wind, “until his judgement inevitably arrives. You’ll know not when, but it is coming.”
item.content:encoded:
“Enjoy your remaining time as ‘guests’ in my lord’s realm,” said Rohash, Lord of the East Wind, “until his judgement inevitably arrives. You’ll know not when, but it is coming.”

He said it from a column of fire and whirlwind beneath a white stone arch on the Rohashi Spires, with Parzelle Starfall close enough to feel the heat. A moment before, High Priestess Lorthuna, who had brought down the wards that hid Zephras Isle and lit a beacon for the Windlord’s court, had asked to be presented to Al’Akir as the one who told him. “Well,” Rohash said, “you certainly never will again, insect.” Then he struck her out into the endless sky.

The chronicler has seen a great many zealots meet the god they prayed to. It almost never goes the way the sermons promised.

It began that afternoon on the eastern road out of Valanaar, where Valennia Stormfist gathered the Peacekeepers for one last look at each other before they marched on the Shrine of Akir. Her plan was the honest kind: a few good fighters through the front to make noise, the bulk of her strength through the flank, punch through quickly and take the High Priestess. Parzelle’s orders were the simplest a captain ever gives. Get in there and start cracking skulls.

The shrine killed her first. The Al’Aketh Guardians at its door are not the Stormcallers of Falaath; they are what the cult keeps for when sermons fail. She came back. A Skyborne named Selenic fell in beside her for a while among the Spiritcallers and Blademasters, then went their own way before the steps, as travellers do. At the top, Hyusaa Quickbreeze, Valennia’s second, said the thing no veteran wants said aloud. This was almost too easy.

Inside, the Sanctum of Storms had gone quiet. Parzelle found Valennia at the top of the spiral stair, cut down and barely conscious. Lorthuna had fled through a portal to the spires, she said; Ayessa Dawnsinger and Supreme Magister Evengale had gone after her; she herself had taken one too many hits, and this was where she stayed. Parzelle stepped through. The sanctum killed her on the way, for good measure.

On the spires, after Rohash’s little speech, the sky sent malevolent storms to see the guests off, and they killed her twice. Four deaths in one afternoon, and the cult’s leader finished not by a young mage’s fire but by the wind she worshipped. Zephras does not hand out clean victories. It hands out survivors.

By evening it was done. Elaadrin Evengale met her in Valanaar. Valennia was resting in the High Elder’s residence. The wards were gone, and Ansirem had told him enough about the elemental lords to know what that meant: if Al’Akir came, the Skyborne could not stand against him in his own domain. “We will find the means to save our home,” he said. “I swear it.” High Elder Talaanis Shadowsong gave the High Order’s expedition her blessing, and Parzelle her own. Winds be with you.

So she went down to the dock outside the lodge and boarded a skycutter.

The chronicler has watched many young people leave home. Few do it by sky. The ship came down over Hillsbrad Foothills in late gold light, over forests that still look the way Lordaeron did before the plague, across a shoulder of the Alterac Mountains, and into Dalaran, where Denaaris Stargale of the High Order was waiting with a speech about how big the world is down here. There is a thing called the Alliance, Denaaris explained, the way one explains snow. Its heart is Stormwind, to the south, and its regent lord, a human named Bolvar Fordragon, would like to meet one of Zephras’s people.

One portal in the Sky Enclave later, Parzelle stood in the Wizard’s Sanctum of Stormwind City, candles guttering on the bookshelves, the portal still glowing behind her.

She has not gone to the regent yet. Stormwind handed her an errand first: Jennea Cannon’s flask, the waterfall at Mirror Lake southwest of the city gates, and a water sample to test for magical taint. The flow of magic in Elwynn has gone wrong, Jennea says. Parzelle comes from an island whose winds went wrong. She may know more about this than the humans do.

Bolvar Fordragon is waiting in his keep. Somewhere above Skywall, so is the Windlord. Neither has said for how long.

item.title: A Word from the Chronicler, Concerning Pace
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Some mornings of late you have woken to find three, even four new tales nailed to the door of this house, each one still wet with ink. That is the trouble with keeping the histories of so many wanderers at once. They do not take turns, and the Chronicler’s hand only has so many fingers.
item.content:encoded:
Some mornings of late you have woken to find three, even four new tales nailed to the door of this house, each one still wet with ink. That is the trouble with keeping the histories of so many wanderers at once. They do not take turns, and the Chronicler’s hand only has so many fingers.

So, for a time, a new custom. One tale a day, set down in the order the deeds were done. On days when many of our travelers each took only a few small steps, their doings will share a single page, a dispatch from across Azeroth rather than a flood of scraps. The greater deeds will still have pages of their own.

Nothing is lost. Every road walked will be written. It will simply arrive at a pace a reader can keep, with time for a cup of something between chapters.

We shall see how it serves. If it chafes, the Chronicler can always go back to drowning you.

item.title: What the River Kept
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Andric died in the river with his boots full of it. Not to a warlord, not to a witch, but to a murloc forager, the small ordinary kind that grubs along the bank for whatever the current brings down. It caught him knee-deep in the reeds south of the Eastvale road and held on longer than he did. The chronicler has recorded grander deaths. Few wetter.
item.content:encoded:
Andric died in the river with his boots full of it. Not to a warlord, not to a witch, but to a murloc forager, the small ordinary kind that grubs along the bank for whatever the current brings down. It caught him knee-deep in the reeds south of the Eastvale road and held on longer than he did. The chronicler has recorded grander deaths. Few wetter.

He got up again. They always do, the ones in this chronicle. He went back into the water.

He had come for Ormin Pelford’s tools. Ormin had been bringing a supply shipment home from the trading post when his wagon tipped over by Brackwell Pumpkin Patch and the whole load went into the river. By the time he reached the bank, the current had carried off an axe, a saw and a toolbox. “Between the murlocs and wolves down there,” he said, “I don’t stand a chance.” Then he looked at Andric and decided he was the hardy sort. People keep deciding things like that about Andric. He keeps letting them.

So the priest the Cathedral of Light sent away for tending the wrong wounded went wading after a woodsman’s toolbox. The chronicler does not think this beneath him. A man who believes every people on Azeroth belongs to one family has to believe in carpenters too.

The saw was first, caught in the rocks and tall reeds a little south of the bridge. The axe was next, on the small island where the river splits, among the mud huts of the murlocs who have claimed it. The toolbox had gone farthest and sunk deepest, down beside a wreck on the river bottom where Elwynn stops and something darker begins. Andric came up for air on the wrong side. The Darkened Bank, the maps call it: the first wet edge of Duskwood, where the trees grow close and the light doesn’t argue with them. He did not stay. He went back toward the pumpkin fields as if the border were a door he had opened by mistake, then through it again, and back once more. The river does not care which kingdom it runs through.

Something in that water had been waiting for him. The murlocs of that camp keep a big one called Croaky, who throws lightning like a shaman and has been making the roads unsafe for longer than anyone has bothered to count. Croaky found Andric at the Darkened Bank with a bolt already crackling in his hands.

Here the record goes thin, and the chronicler will not fill it with heroics he did not see. A traveller named Mystic, out of Frostwhisper, came along the bank and stood with Andric for a few minutes, then went his own way. Afterwards there were five more murloc fins in Andric’s pack for Guard Thomas’s bounty, and, a little later, a head. Croaky’s. Draw your own conclusions. The chronicler has drawn his: the roads south of Eastvale are a little safer tonight, and a priest who heals for a living has a murloc’s head wrapped in cloth among his things.

The chronicler has wondered, not aloud, whether Andric’s one family of Azeroth’s peoples includes murlocs. Andric has not said. The murlocs did not ask.

Back at the pumpkin patch, Ormin took the axe, the saw and the toolbox and looked him over. “You look a bit damp,” he said. “Sorry about that. But thank you for retrieving the supplies.” That was the whole of it. Stormwind remembered the favor, in the small way Stormwind remembers things, and Andric walked off up the road at dusk with four silver he hadn’t had that morning and not a copper spent.

The head is supposed to go to Merell Ross at Ridgepoint Tower, on the road toward Redridge, because the watch will want to know. Thomas still wants three more fins. And the satchel is getting heavy: a murloc’s head, a letter for Gryan Stoutmantle in Westfall that nobody has delivered, and a little bottle meant to make Maybell Maclure invisible to her own family, still wrapped in cloth, still waiting for Andric to decide whether helping her leave is a kindness. The river gave back the tools. It has not given him an answer.

item.title: The Breaker at the Bottom of the Hill
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: “Valennia only sent one person to help repel a full-scale assault,” Yorana Windyreed had said, looking Parzelle Starfall over at the East Pylon Watchtower. “By the winds. You don’t look like much, but I’ll take what I can get.”
item.content:encoded:
“Valennia only sent one person to help repel a full-scale assault,” Yorana Windyreed had said, looking Parzelle Starfall over at the East Pylon Watchtower. “By the winds. You don’t look like much, but I’ll take what I can get.”

The last time the chronicler wrote of the Gustberry Lowlands, Parzelle died in them before the sun was fully up. She came back down the same hill that evening.

The Al’Aketh were still there, of course. Cults don’t go home because someone died fighting them. Their healers worked among the trees, keeping the brawlers on their feet and the assault rolling toward the watchtower, and Yorana’s plan was the oldest one in any siege: kill the people who keep the attackers coming, and the attack runs out of breath. Parzelle went looking for healers. She found four, and eight brawlers besides, and somewhere in the middle of them, under the gnarled trees with the cultists closing in, the arcane settled deeper into her. She stood up out of that fight a little more dangerous than she had knelt down in it. The chronicler has watched a great many young mages learn that power arrives at inconvenient moments. It rarely asks whether you are busy.

Then the villa. Commander Belguilos, they call her the Breaker. She was a peacekeeper once, before the cult got out of hand, and even then, Yorana said, she was off. Yorana had sent Parzelle after her at first light, knowing she might be sending her to her death, and had been right. The Breaker kept to an upper room of a house at the base of the hill, as if the war below were weather.

Parzelle climbed the stairs.

The chronicler will not describe what he did not see. He can report what came after: Parzelle walked back up to the East Pylon Watchtower with the healers thinned and the Breaker dead, and Yorana, who had a greeting ready for the cult and none for her, said it anyway. “Storms curse these Al’Aketh fanatics!” Then she paid her, and thanked her in the manner of a soldier who has stopped expecting help to arrive. Seven silver and change. Not a copper spent. The whole business took less time than a good supper.

There is a satisfaction in it the chronicler won’t pretend away. The Lowlands killed her once. Parzelle went back down and broke the woman who ran them. Revenge is a poor reason to fight, the old songs say, but it is a fine reason to climb a staircase.

Still, the question Constable Aonda asked has not gone anywhere: what does the Al’Aketh want with so many windstones? Parzelle carries four of their charms toward a count of ten. Resaan’s heirloom is still somewhere on the island, and the refugees’ belongings are still scattered in the grass. And Yorana has sent her home to Valanaar, where Supreme Magister Evengale will tell her, no doubt, that he would have preferred less blood. He always does. Someone always spills it anyway.

item.title: Eggs for Xar’Ti
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The makrura came up out of the surf on Darkspear Strand like the sea had sent its rubbish back, all claws and clacking plates, and Tazu met them in the shallows with lightning in one hand and a stone mace in the other. Somewhere in the middle of it, with the water pink in the evening light and a clacker going still at his feet, the spirits leaned on him again. Light rose through him from the sand up. He came out of it stronger than he went in, the way you do when the world decides you have earned a little more of it. The makrura did not notice. Makrura notice very little.
item.content:encoded:
The makrura came up out of the surf on Darkspear Strand like the sea had sent its rubbish back, all claws and clacking plates, and Tazu met them in the shallows with lightning in one hand and a stone mace in the other. Somewhere in the middle of it, with the water pink in the evening light and a clacker going still at his feet, the spirits leaned on him again. Light rose through him from the sand up. He came out of it stronger than he went in, the way you do when the world decides you have earned a little more of it. The makrura did not notice. Makrura notice very little.

He was there for Master Vornal. Vornal is the old alchemist of Sen’jin Village, whose eyes are failing and whose temper is not. He has never taken an apprentice, because no troll or orc has ever come to him worthy enough. “Are you worthy?” he asks the young ones who wander up to his fire. “Yes, of course you are… of course you think you are.” Then he sends them down to the shore for intact makrura eyes and vials of crawler mucus, which is the kind of errand that tells a master a great deal about a student.

Tazu brought him four eyes and eight vials. “Well done, young one,” Vornal said. “Well done indeed.” Then he paid him in really sticky glue, ten pots of it, which the chronicler suspects is Vornal’s idea of a joke. Orgrimmar and the Darkspear both took note. Vornal has a saying for those who keep him waiting: time is the true test of your strength and will, and if you lose patience or give in to weakness, your true self will be shown. The earth at Spirit Rock told Tazu much the same thing, not long ago. Be patient. Remain strong. The spirits, it seems, have been talking to the old men of Sen’jin.

Then there was Xar’Ti. Every raptor in the pens outside Sen’jin is one Xar’Ti trained, and they come from all over Kalimdor, but some of the finest come from the Bloodtalons on the Echo Isles. One of those, the Bloodtalon Matriarch, had grown too savage to leave at the village’s borders. She had killed trolls from Sen’jin. Xar’Ti wanted her dead, and wanted her eggs brought home, so the hatchlings could be raised as allies instead of enemies.

The chronicler did not see the Matriarch fall. He only saw Tazu walk up to the pens at sunset with her eggs, and Xar’Ti take them, and the swift raptors in their saddles turn their heads to watch. There is something about it the chronicler keeps coming back to. A mother killed for being too dangerous, and her children carried home to be taught better. The Darkspear are a practical people. Xar’Ti gave Tazu a pair of raptorscale trousers for his trouble, and the chronicler hopes, for the hatchlings’ sake, that none of them ever learns where the leather came from.

Three hundred and eighty-five coppers by nightfall. No deaths. He made camp in Durotar.

A report is owed to Orgnil in Razor Hill. A peon’s burden is ready to be set down. And somewhere in Durotar the Kolkar centaurs have drawn up plans to strike at the Valley of Trials, Sen’jin Village and Orgrimmar itself. Tazu has burned one of them. Two are still out there, and the centaurs do not know yet that a patient troll is looking for them.

item.title: The Spirits Have Guided You
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The fire was already burning when he found it: a small ring of stones and a tripod of blackened poles, set in the red dirt of a valley that had been waiting for him. The sky over Durotar was the color of a banked coal. The cliffs held the heat of the day and gave it back.
item.content:encoded:
The fire was already burning when he found it: a small ring of stones and a tripod of blackened poles, set in the red dirt of a valley that had been waiting for him. The sky over Durotar was the color of a banked coal. The cliffs held the heat of the day and gave it back.

The chronicler will admit to a little invention here, because the record does not say how Tazu came to be standing in that valley, only that he did. He is a Darkspear, one of the trolls who crossed the sea with Thrall’s Horde and were given this hard, red country for a home. The village sent him to the Valley of Trials the way the Darkspear have always sent their young: to find out whether the spirits would have him. He had already decided that the earth under Durotar’s dirt was talking. He had come to learn how to answer it.

The first errand had a name that sounded like a joke until it didn’t. Your Place in the World. It led him into The Den, to Gornek, who looked him over and, being an honest orc, declined to send a new recruit into the Barrens after kodo. “In all honesty,” Gornek said, “you’re more useful to us alive than dead.” He sent Tazu north instead, after the mottled boars. Cutting Teeth.

Tazu cut them. Midway through the work the strength came up through him in a column of gold light, the way it does in the first days. On the way back he stopped under the canopy outside the Den and learned the first of his trades from Zor’la: how to find the herbs that grow in this dry country, and how to take them without wasting them. He took up skinning as well. A shaman who cannot feed himself is only a man talking to the wind.

Gornek took the boars’ proof and handed him a rune-inscribed tablet, and a second chore: scorpid tails from the valley. Tazu carried the tablet to Shikrik, the shaman trainer who stands in the sun just outside the Den, with Canaga Earthcaller not far off. “The spirits have guided you to me,” she said. “How may I be of service?” He asked her to teach him the ways of the spirits. She put Rockbiter on his weapon, the blessing that makes a mace feel like stone.

The valley does not empty after one errand. He gathered abandoned training weapons from the dirt and brought them home to the Den. Galgar, who keeps a fire under the same canopy as Zor’la, wanted cactus apples for a surprise. Zureetha Fargaze sent him after the vile familiars that come down from the Burning Blade’s cave in the rocks. And on a low ridge, an injured troll named Hana’zua asked him to kill the scorpid that had put him there. The scorpid was called Sarkoth.

The scorpids took their share of the morning. He walked the red canyons with lightning in his right hand and a mace that had learned to bite like stone, picking cactus apples as he went, and came up to level three in a narrow cut in the rock.

Tazu killed Sarkoth. Hana’zua, who could not walk back to the Den, asked him to take the news to Gornek. “Seeing the deed you have done for me steels my heart,” he said. “I cannot fall so easily! I must endure!” The chronicler records the speech as it was given, and also that Tazu did not die once in the doing of any of it.

He came up to level four among the familiars in the rocks, then brought the work home. He turned the apples in to Galgar and came away with a stack of cactus apple surprise and a little coin. He turned the scorpid tails in to Gornek, and Hana’zua’s message with them. Canaga Earthcaller, who had been waiting, gave him the first real work of a shaman: Call of Earth. Shikrik taught him Earth Shock, a short, hard strike that starts in the ground. Zureetha took the proof of the familiars and sent him on. There is a medallion in the Burning Blade coven, in a cave to the north and west, and she wants it brought out. “Go, Tazu,” she said.

He accepted one more chore before he sat down: Lazy Peons. Then he logged out in the Valley of Trials, level four, thirty-four minutes after he had found the fire. The earth quest is still in his pack, unfinished. The medallion is still in the cave. The peons, the chronicler assumes, are still lazy.

The spirits have guided him this far. The valley is not done with him.

item.title: Be Patient, Tazu
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The stone spoke first. It does that, at Spirit Rock, if you have walked to the end of the Hidden Path with a sapta in your hand and the sense to drink it there and nowhere else.
item.content:encoded:
The stone spoke first. It does that, at Spirit Rock, if you have walked to the end of the Hidden Path with a sapta in your hand and the sense to drink it there and nowhere else.

What rose to meet Tazu was not a stone so much as a quarrel of stones: black slabs veined with red heat, hanging in the air around a grey standing rock as if the ground had decided to stand up and look at him. It looked. Then it gave him a pebble.

“Be patient, Tazu,” the earth said. “Remain strong. And seek wisdom. This is what earth asks of you. In the end, you shall become one with the earth. Respect it as it shall respect you.”

The chronicler has heard a great many spirits make a great many speeches. Most of them want something killed. This one wanted patience, which is a harder errand and pays worse.

He had earned the audience the long way round. The afternoon began back in the Burning Blade’s cave, the coven in the rocks north and west of the Den, where the cult that keeps sending familiars down into the Valley of Trials hides the things it values. Somewhere in that dark the strength came up through him again, the way it does when a young troll survives things that were meant to stop him. When he came out, he had Zureetha Fargaze’s medallion. She took it with the air of a seer who had expected exactly this, and who also expected the Burning Blade to have further plans for Durotar. Seers are rarely wrong about that. They are rarely cheerful either.

There was smaller business. Foreman Thazz’ril’s peons had been sleeping on the job, and Tazu woke them, which is the sort of heroism nobody sings about. Thazz’ril, pleased, called him a dependable troll and handed him another task: a favorite pick, left behind in that same cave in a chamber with waterfalls, now guarded by things the foreman would rather not discuss. Tazu took the job. He did not go back for the pick. It is, as far as this record knows, still down there in the dark, glowing faintly with the spell the foreman put on it so it could be found.

Then Canaga Earthcaller. He brought her the felstalker hooves she had asked for, and she gave him the sapta and the road to Spirit Rock. He walked it, drank, listened, and came back with the rough quartz. Canaga did what earthcallers do with such a pebble, and Tazu learned to set a totem in the dirt that hardens the skin of those who stand near it. Stone, it turns out, can be shared.

He accepted one more charge before he rested, a summons titled simply The Adventurer, and made camp in Durotar four hundred seventy coppers richer.

Between that afternoon and the night, the record goes quiet. When it picks up again he was stronger than when it left him, standing on the far side of Durotar, near the water.

The Echo Isles sit off the coast below Sen’jin Village. The Darkspear came ashore there when they first reached Kalimdor, and it was meant to be home. Then the witch doctor Zalazane took the largest isle with his hexes and made his own people into his servants, and the tribe withdrew to the mainland to watch the islands it had lost. Tazu crossed over at night, under a sky the color of an old bruise.

He did not go entirely alone. For a while two other adventurers walked with him, and for a while one of them did not. By the end he was by himself again. The isles have that effect on company.

He came back with a great deal. A skull, first: Minshina’s, taken from Zalazane’s circle of power, where the witch doctor had trapped a dead troll’s spirit inside his own bones. Master Gadrin, whose brother it was, took it in Sen’jin Village. “I thank you, Tazu,” he said. “And my brother thanks you.” The light rose through Tazu again as he said it, and the chronicler will not pretend the timing was anything but fitting.

Then the rest. Zalazane’s head, for Gadrin, and with it an end to the hexes. Forgotten loa idols, brought back from wherever the isles had been hiding them. And four Durotar tiger furs for Vel’rin Fang, who needs hides for blankets and tents before the seasons turn. Four hundred and five coppers. No deaths. He made camp in Durotar, a whole coastline from the valley where he had found the fire.

The earth told him to be patient. He has been, mostly. There is still a pick in a cave with waterfalls, a summons in his pack he has not answered, and an island that was home to his people, quieter tonight than it has been in years. The spirits are watching to see what he does with that.

item.title: Lightning over Falaath
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The Stormcaller ran. The chronicler wants that on the record first, because it is the part Parzelle Starfall will remember with the most satisfaction. One of the Al’Aketh’s lightning-priests, robes snapping in a wind he believed belonged to him, took one look at the fire in her hands, lost his nerve, and fled across the meadow below Falaath Village.
item.content:encoded:
The Stormcaller ran. The chronicler wants that on the record first, because it is the part Parzelle Starfall will remember with the most satisfaction. One of the Al’Aketh’s lightning-priests, robes snapping in a wind he believed belonged to him, took one look at the fire in her hands, lost his nerve, and fled across the meadow below Falaath Village.

Then the lightning came down anyway, and she died in the grass.

That is the whole of the morning, more or less, and it was a short morning. She came back to the Shen’dar Highlands with a peacekeeper’s bloody note still in her satchel and the cult’s village still in front of her. Havoc in the Highlands and Stolen Supplies were both waiting, and both pointed the same direction: down the green slope to Falaath, where the Al’Aketh preach that the island’s winds can be bargained with, and steal Shen’dar Village’s food to keep the sermon going.

She did not go alone. A fellow traveller fell in beside her, and the two of them walked into Falaath together. The chronicler has watched a great many first partnerships on a great many islands. Most of them last exactly as long as the next fight. This one lasted the morning, which is better than most.

Falaath is not a fortress. It is worse: a village, with cookfires and bread, where people who were once ordinary Skyborne now stand in the doorways with storm in their fingers. The Stormcallers fight the way the cult thinks, which is to say they do not argue with you. They call a cloud down over your head and let the sky do the arguing. Parzelle traded fire and arcane for their shocks, and for a while she was winning. Fireball. Arcane Missiles. A Stormcaller fleeing in terror. The fallen left behind a strip of galestrider jerky and a cracked windstone, which is what the Al’Aketh carry instead of good sense.

Then the cloud found her.

The chronicler does not dress deaths up. She lay in the long grass under a bright sky, a few strides from a pale carcass in the meadow, while the shadows of the trees crossed her like bars. Her companion stood over her. The Stormcallers went back to their doorways.

Twelve minutes. Ninety-nine copper. One death, which on Zephras Isle is less an ending than an argument about who gets the last word.

The supplies are still stolen. The havoc is still loose in the highlands. The peacekeeper’s note is still folded in her satchel, still unanswered. And the Al’Aketh have learned something useful about the young mage from the High Order: that she can make them run, and that she can still be brought down. The chronicler suspects she has learned the same two things about them.

item.title: The Keep on the Bluffs
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: “Another fresh recruit? Welcome to Bandarion Keep, brother.”
item.content:encoded:
“Another fresh recruit? Welcome to Bandarion Keep, brother.”

Breton Samuels said it in a stone hall that smelled of damp mortar and old murloc, and Ghoulsbie stood there with a mallet across his back and the Brill road still on his boots. Nobody had called him brother since the grave. The chronicler watched him decide whether to believe it. He did not decide.

He had come a long way round to get there.

The day began in Brill, where it always begins, with errands. William Pickman finished teaching him to cook at Gallows’ End Tavern. Shari Stilwell, who had been waiting to continue his training, finally did, and sent him out with a new rebuke in his hands: a hammer of judgment that stops a man where he stands, and the gift of making a poisoned body clean. The laced pumpkin went down to the cellar, to the Captured Scarlet Zealot who did not know what he was about to eat. Apothecary Johaan got his darkhound blood, and later his murloc scales, and then asked for spider venom. Ghoulsbie has met the spiders of Tirisfal. He accepted anyway.

Gordo’s gloom weed led to Junior Apothecary Holland’s Doom Weed, which led to Holland asking for Tomb Weed. The Royal Apothecary Society names its errands the way it names its plagues: honestly, and with relish.

Then the gnolls. Garren’s Haunt sits north of Brill, and in it Maggot Eye, a Rot Hide brute with a price on his head. Ghoulsbie collected the paw. Executor Zygand collected the paw from Ghoulsbie and paid him. Magistrate Sevren wanted the Rot Hide graverobbers thinned as well, and their embalming ichor brought home, because in Brill even the grave-thieves have something worth taking. Sevren rewarded him with more work: orders for Bethor Iceshard in the Undercity, the Haunted Mills, the remains of the Agamand family to be gathered up for Coleman Farthing. He passed Agamand Mills on the way, quiet, for now.

And then Shari Stilwell gave him a different kind of errand. A new paladin order, she said, was taking root in Tirisfal. Risen paladins. Forsaken who still answer to the Light. They had a monastery on the bluffs northwest of Solliden Farmstead, at the edge of the Whispering Woods. It was called Bandarion Keep, and it was hard to miss.

It was not hard to miss. Ghoulsbie found it the long way, past Stillwater Pond, and arrived to discover the order’s first problem was not the Light at all. It was murlocs. The Vile Fin had used the keep as a spawning ground before the paladins moved in, and they had not accepted the eviction. Breton put him to work before he put him up. He cleared the attackers off the bluffs and the seers out of the lakeside camps, and somewhere along the road he felt himself grow harder to kill. The murlocs will be back. Breton said as much. It is hard enough rebuilding a fortress without a murloc trying to put a spear in your back.

He toured the grounds after that, and met Danitha Morr, who calls herself the closest thing the keep has to a commander. She did not pretend it was much. She told him the truth instead: the order is mistrusted by its own people, who remember well what the living did to them in the name of the Light. And some risen paladins never left their old hatreds in the grave. The Tarnished, she calls them. They have dug in at Shadowvale, and they kill Forsaken, and every killing makes it easier to believe the whole order is the same. She wants them ended, and their commander’s head brought back. Jorin Croge, meanwhile, wants lumber. Fortresses on bluffs are hard to supply. Location, he said, is everything.

The chronicler would note that Ghoulsbie had already met one paladin who could not bear what she had become, west of Deathknell, and granted her the end she asked for. Danitha’s Tarnished are the other answer to the same question. They chose to stay, and to keep hating.

He had met a third answer earlier that evening, at Crusader’s Outpost. Bareth Dawnstone, a brother of the keep, had been taken on the road to Brill by men who wield the Light with hatred in their hearts. Ghoulsbie got him out. A stranger fought beside him for a few minutes, then went their own way, the way strangers do. Shari Stilwell, back in Brill, blessed him for it. And Brill being Brill, the Scarlets had also been dealt with, so Zygand paid him and immediately named a Scarlet captain he wanted dead.

Somewhere in there he also signed a company roll. The Goblin News Network, which listed him as a Corporate Asset. The dead do not get to choose their titles.

The last thing he did in the daylight was report to Deathguard Linnea, who gave him a patrol, a hide order and a message for the magistrate. Then he died. The chronicle does not say what killed him. It records only that the next place he stood was the Ruins of Lordaeron, among the broken walls of the capital his old life had served, and that he went down beneath them into the Undercity and walked the Canals for the first time.

Sevren’s orders for Bethor Iceshard are still in his pack. The Tarnished are still at Shadowvale. The keep is still half a ruin with murlocs at the gate. He has a place to sleep there now, if he wants it. He has not said whether he does.

item.title: Stormapples for a Lost Cause
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: “Stranger… please… put me down… on the bedroll by that tree there…”
item.content:encoded:
“Stranger… please… put me down… on the bedroll by that tree there…”

Fillion Flamebreeze said it from somewhere over Parzelle Starfall’s shoulder, because that is where she was carrying him. The High Order’s missing scholar weighed more than a scholar ought to, and bled more than he admitted to. She put him down on the bedroll by the tree. The chronicler has seen worse rescues. Not many more polite ones.

But the day did not begin with a rescue. It began, as her last one ended, with the grass of Falaath Village and her own body in it. Falaath had brought her down a second time. The fellow traveller who had walked into Falaath with her was gone a few minutes later. Partnerships on Zephras Isle last as long as the next fight; this one had lasted two.

She went back anyway. When she came up the hill to Shen’dar Village again, the stolen supplies were in her packs, the havoc in the highlands had been answered, and the peacekeeper’s bloody note had been read aloud to Constable Aonda. “So they are all dead, then,” Aonda said, and cursed the cult, and asked the question no one on the island can yet answer: what does the Al’Aketh want with so many windstones?

Aonda sent her down to Valanaar with a report and a ring. The ring was the Shadowsong family signet, recovered from the tower, and it went to Talaanis Shadowsong, High Elder of Zephras Isle. He saw what she was holding before she spoke. “Oh… oh no.” He thanked her anyway. Good men usually do.

Valanaar is where the island keeps its politics. Elaadrin Evengale, Supreme Magister of the High Order, received her in the lodge and told her she had a vibrant arcane aura, which is the sort of thing the powerful say to the useful. He told her the plan as well: rediscover the lost magic of their forebears, build lanes through the elemental plane, and find Azeroth again. The Kirin Tor will show the way, he said. Then he sent her to find his scholar.

She found Fillion’s satchel first, on the road west, with blood on the flap. Then the cave to the north: the Shriekling Den. The Windshapers had ambushed him on his way back from the Overlook Standing Stones, he said, and left him bleeding at the cave mouth for something with wings to carry off. Something had. It was the Shriekling Matriarch’s nest, and Parzelle came out of it with more power in her hands than she went in with, and later went back in for the Matriarch’s head.

Fillion’s lost data mattered, it turned out. Without it the skycutters cannot steer between Skywall and Azeroth. Evengale sent Parzelle to the Overlook Standing Stones with an Index Esoteria to read the windstones herself, and told her that if the Windshapers objected, she should do what she needed to do. When she came back with the readings, he said it would not have been his preference to spill Windshaper blood, and that they were already calling it a massacre. The chronicler records what the Supreme Magister said. The chronicler also notes who did the spilling, and who did the preferring.

Between those errands, a man named Alvarion Windfield, wounded and wincing, asked whether she wanted work, and sent her west to his orchard and his wife. Aamelia Windfield heard the story out and told Parzelle the truth: “I think my idiot husband likely just sent you here to die for nothing. If you have any sense at all, you should leave now.”

She did not have that kind of sense. She picked stormapples. She killed the bandits who came early to skim the harvest before their leader, Ferauu, came for the rest. She took tenderloins from the ornery galestriders and dust from the flutterflies, and stopped to listen to a rusted Cyclone Construct that has wandered the fields since the wind elementals left, asking the same broken question over and over. What is… Nobody has answered it in a thousand years.

Then she took the bandits’ masks, and when there was nothing left to prepare, Aamelia offered her one last chance to walk away. She stayed. A stranger stood with them too, for the end of it. And then it was over, and Aamelia had to sit down before her heart left her chest.

Parzelle carried the news back to Alvarion, who wept, and called her a real hero, like the stories from before they came to Skywall. Aamelia told her one more thing, quietly, about why that construct had to be made safe. She was asked to keep it. The chronicler is keeping it too.

Belann Windwood taught her the old tradition: a young mage gathers a wind-touched bough from the oldest trees by the shrine below Falaath and shapes her own focus from it. She learned to freeze the ground beneath an enemy’s feet. She told Valennia Stormfist that the High Order stood with Valanaar against the Al’Aketh, and Valennia said the dead mage, Belathaan, had been her cousin.

At first light the cult hit the east pylon watchtower. Yorana Windyreed was holding, barely. Down the hill the cult’s healers kept the attackers coming, and somewhere among them a commander called Belguilos the Breaker, who used to be a peacekeeper. Parzelle went down the hill.

She died in the Gustberry Lowlands before the sun was fully up. The Breaker is still waiting at the villa at the bottom of the hill. So is everyone who ever thought the winds took sides.

item.title: The Bottle William Pestle Poured
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The bottle was small, and the liquid in it did not want to be looked at. William Pestle pressed it into Andric’s hands across a table at the Lion’s Pride Inn and explained, with the calm of an apothecary who has stopped asking questions, that it was for Maybell Maclure.
