item.content:encoded:
The bottle was small, and the liquid in it did not want to be looked at. William Pestle pressed it into Andric’s hands across a table at the Lion’s Pride Inn and explained, with the calm of an apothecary who has stopped asking questions, that it was for Maybell Maclure. One swallow and a girl can walk out of her father’s house without her father seeing. One swallow and she can reach the Stonefield farm and Tommy Joe.

The chronicler has noted before that Andric spent an evening running pies between two families who will not share a fence. Now he is carrying the means of escape for one of their daughters. He did not take it to her. Not yet. He put it in his satchel and walked east, which is either wisdom or cowardice, and in the chronicler’s experience the two are usually wearing each other’s coats.

East is the Eastvale Logging Camp, past Guard Thomas’s post and over the bridge, where the great trees of Elwynn come down one at a time and the Stormwind Army keeps a tailor on retainer. Her name is Sara Timberlain. Andric had earned a marker from the army, good for one piece of armor, and Sara turned it into a well-stitched robe. Whether he will trade the white Friar’s Robes of the Light for it, the chronicler cannot say. A man who was sent away from the Cathedral tends to be sentimental about the first vestments anyone gave him since.

Sara had another request. The Defias gangs in Northshire wear burlap masks, she said, but the ones in Elwynn wear red linen, and good linen is good linen. Bring her red bandanas and she will make something fine from them. She said it the way you would talk about wool. The chronicler watched Andric’s face while she said it, and will only report that he accepted.

They were masons once, some of those men. He bandaged them in the cellars of Old Town. Now their bandanas are tailoring stock.

Supervisor Raelen had the oldest problem in any logging camp: a deadline. The wolves and bears north of the camp had chased her cutters away from wood they had already felled, and the lumber order would not wait. Andric went into the trees and carried the bundles back. Raelen paid him three silver and told everyone within earshot that they still had not met their quota. A logging camp is not a place for gratitude. It is a place for the next tree.

At the same camp, Hagar Lowe told him that good steel is scarce since the war and that the Jasperlode miners left fine picks behind in the dark when they fled. Would he fetch some? Andric said he would. The chronicler is beginning to suspect he has never said no to anyone in his life, which may be exactly why the Cathedral found him so inconvenient.

Then Guard Thomas, at the east bridge, where the prowlers and the young forest bears had been pressing the frontier. Andric cleared enough of them that Thomas called it done. A priest is supposed to mend things, and the chronicler supposes a wolf that will not reach the logging camp is a kind of mending. Thomas had no medallions to hand him this time. He had a bounty instead. The Stormwind Army wants murloc fins from the village at Stone Cairn Lake and from another one where the stream forks to the south.

Stone Cairn Lake. Where he found Rolf in the reeds, and learned the prayer that raises the dead on the same night it was too late to use it.

Thirty-two minutes on the road. Fourteen silver and change, and not a copper spent. Andric is going back to the lake. The red bandanas are waiting on Defias necks. Hagar’s picks are in the Jasperlode dark. Gryan Stoutmantle’s letter is still in his pack, unread by anyone in Westfall. And in the same satchel, a little bottle that makes a girl invisible to her own family sits wrapped in cloth, while the man carrying it, who believes every people on Azeroth is one family, tries to decide whether helping someone leave hers is a kindness.

item.title: Paxton’s Last Two Books
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Fargodeep Mine smells of tallow, wet stone and kobold, in that order, and the order changes the deeper you go. Tristan Ludlowe went deep. He came back up with a book called Fun with Elementals, which is not, the chronicler is assured, a children’s primer, and which Brother Paxton has been losing sleep over since the day the kobolds carried it out of Northshire.
item.content:encoded:
Fargodeep Mine smells of tallow, wet stone and kobold, in that order, and the order changes the deeper you go. Tristan Ludlowe went deep. He came back up with a book called Fun with Elementals, which is not, the chronicler is assured, a children’s primer, and which Brother Paxton has been losing sleep over since the day the kobolds carried it out of Northshire.

He did not go down alone, for a while. Another adventurer fell in beside him in the dark of the mine and they worked the tunnels together, the way strangers do in Fargodeep: without names, without speeches, and without much choice. Then the stranger went their own way. The mine does that to partnerships. Tristan kept going.

He had come from Stormwind that evening, out of the Trade District, the same streets where the sergeant keeps his recruiting table. If he looked for the man on his way out of the city, the chronicler did not see it. He walked out through the gates, down into Elwynn, and into the ground.

The mine gave up more than the book. The kobolds of Fargodeep carry gold dust in their pouches, which Remy “Two Times” had wanted, twice. They carry large candles on their heads, which William Pestle wanted for reasons the chronicler did not ask. Tristan scouted the mine for Marshal Dughan, then walked back through the Maclure Vineyards, where the grapes grow up against a family feud and the Defias walk the rows.

Back in Goldshire, the strength came again. One more rung on the ladder. Remy took the gold dust in a flare of golden light and paid him with a bag of marbles, which tells you everything about Remy you need to know. Dughan took the scouting report on Fargodeep and immediately gave him another, for the Jasperlode Mine to the northeast. Dughan has a gift for that. Pestle took the candles and handed him a shipment for his brother Morgan in Stormwind’s Trade District. Back to the Trade District, then. Back past the table.

And Dughan, holding Fun with Elementals at arm’s length, told him the worst of it. Paxton’s list is not finished. Two books are still missing: Geomancy for Curious Young Wizards and Arcane Explainer: Magical Stuff in Simple Words. They are in the Jasperlode Mine, and the kobold who has them is no apprentice. If the little one at Fargodeep was summoning elementals, Dughan said, imagine the master. Bring friends.

The chronicler would like it recorded that a kobold in Elwynn is studying geomancy from a picture book, and that this is considered a military matter.

The Light’s trainer in Goldshire taught Tristan two new things that evening. The first was a hammer of the Light that drops a man where he stands and keeps him there. The second was a quieter prayer, one that burns poison and sickness out of a body. One to stop a man. One to save him. The boy keeps being handed both halves of the same lesson, and keeps reaching for the first.

At the Lion’s Pride Inn, Michelle Belle, Goldshire’s physician, showed him how to fold a heavier bandage and pack a proper kit. Someone at the inn taught him to brew a small healing draught besides. Six silver spent on all of it, which for a carter’s son is real money. The chronicler approves of the purchase. Northwatch eats young men who cannot stop their own bleeding.

He came out of the inn into Goldshire’s square at night, where a crier shouted news from beyond the borders and travellers sat around a fire, and just to the south the Darkmoon Faire had raised its striped tents for the week. The Faire took note of him, as it takes note of everyone who comes within earshot of its barkers.

Paxton’s last two books are in Jasperlode, guarded by something that reads. Guard Thomas is still waiting at the eastern bridge. Morgan Pestle is waiting in the Trade District, a short walk from the sergeant’s table. And somewhere past Northwatch, Garret’s letters are still not coming.

item.title: The Road Down to Goldshire
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The kobold at the back of Echo Ridge Mine called himself Shinyfinder Narf, and he was sitting on a sack of picture books like a dragon on a hoard.
item.content:encoded:
The kobold at the back of Echo Ridge Mine called himself Shinyfinder Narf, and he was sitting on a sack of picture books like a dragon on a hoard.

The chronicler would like to report a great battle. It was a mine shaft, a candle-stub of a chieftain and a young man from the Trade District with a wooden mace, and the young man walked out with the sack. Kelsey Fargo, the mining apprentice who keeps watch at the mouth of the mine, had told him the little diggers came through shouting “Picture for Narf!” with Brother Paxton’s library under their arms. Nobody in Northshire knew who Narf was. Now Marshal McBride does, and has the books on his desk to prove it.

It was the end of a long debt to that valley. Tristan cleared the kobold workers camped at the mine, then the laborers inside it, for the Marshal. Somewhere in the middle of it the strength came again, down in the dark of the mine, and he barely stopped to notice.

Deputy Willem got his red bandanas at last, twelve of them, taken off the Defias thugs across the river. Willem had a friend, as deputies always do. Milly Osworth had left her grape harvest sitting in crates in the Northshire Vineyards when the Brotherhood moved in, and she feared the guards would trample it chasing them as surely as the thieves would steal it. Tristan carried the crates out. Then, because a vineyard full of Defias has a man in charge, he went back for Garrick Padfoot, the cutthroat who had been bleeding the valley’s farmers for weeks, and brought his head to Deputy Willem in a sack. The chronicler notes it was the second sack of the evening, and the heavier one.

Milly’s ledger went up the bell tower to Brother Neals, who keeps the abbey’s food and drink and likes to taste the wine himself, purely as a matter of stewardship.

Then the trainer, and this is the part the chronicler keeps turning over. The abbey taught Tristan how to put the Light into a blow and how to call it down on a man to judge him, which is the part of paladinhood the boy came for. It also taught him to pour it into another man’s wounds, and to wrap himself in it when the blows came too fast. Strike and shield and mend, all in one lesson. The sergeant in the Trade District had asked for exactly one of those things.

McBride put papers in his hand and pointed him south, past the border gates. Goldshire was waiting with the same faces it always has. Marshal Dughan took the documents and the kobold tracks Tristan had followed down from the abbey with a dwarf hunter’s tracking kit, and concluded, as Dughan does, that the trouble was bigger than one valley: the Fargodeep Mine to the south is full of kobolds too, and somewhere in it is a book called Fun with Elementals that Brother Paxton is terrified a kobold might learn to read.

A frontiersman named Sam Sarsaparilla had pitched a tent by the road and made him sit by a fire until he felt rested in his bones, then signed him up to cook, mine, gather herbs and fish, all at once. The boy signs things. The chronicler has said so before and will be saying it at his funeral.

At Crystal Lake a fishmonger named Jason Mathers was going broke. His partner Lee had set traps overnight and they came up full of half-eaten fish, and the murlocs on the far shore were to blame. Tristan thinned them out and grew a little stronger on the lakeshore for it. Lee wanted shiny junk from the murloc camp for bait, and paid in his own old fishing gear. Remy “Two Times,” who says everything twice, wants murloc bait brewed from duskweed and animal blood, and swears it is perfectly safe as long as nobody eats it. Marshal Dughan, asked to send soldiers east against the murlocs, declined politely and sent Tristan to the eastern bridge to fetch a report from Guard Thomas instead.

Somewhere in all of it, he learned to roll a linen bandage. Light for the wounds that need it, linen for the ones that don’t. The sergeant would approve.

He ended the night where he began the story: walking up the Valley of Heroes under a violet sky, past the stone giants, into Stormwind. The same city where the recruiters set up their table. He carries a little more of the Light than he did, and a good deal more errands.

Guard Thomas is waiting at the eastern bridge. The Fargodeep Mine is waiting with Paxton’s books. Garret’s letters are still not coming. And somewhere in the Trade District, a sergeant may be looking up from his table to see who just walked in.

item.title: The Note in the Peacekeeper’s Hand
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The body at the western watchtower was still warm enough to be recent. That is the first thing the chronicler wants you to know, because it is the first thing Parzelle Starfall knew. Burns ran along the peacekeeper’s skin in the branching pattern lightning leaves, and the stones around him were scorched the same way. Constable Aonda had sent her to tell Peacekeeper Vaaniel to abandon the tower and fall back to Shen’dar Village. Holding it, the constable said, was not worth the lives it would cost.
item.content:encoded:
The body at the western watchtower was still warm enough to be recent. That is the first thing the chronicler wants you to know, because it is the first thing Parzelle Starfall knew. Burns ran along the peacekeeper’s skin in the branching pattern lightning leaves, and the stones around him were scorched the same way. Constable Aonda had sent her to tell Peacekeeper Vaaniel to abandon the tower and fall back to Shen’dar Village. Holding it, the constable said, was not worth the lives it would cost.

It had already cost his.

A note slid out of his hand when she knelt. It was bloody, folded, and written by a man who knew he was not going to finish the day. Parzelle picked it up. That is all the chronicler can honestly report, because that is where she stopped: on the stones of the West Pylon Watchtower, with the note in her hand, the tower door open behind the dead man, and whatever the Faithful had left inside still waiting for her.

But that was the end of the day. It did not start that way. Most bad days don’t.

It started at Windsong Lake, with a fishing line.

Raan Wildwind, who has decided that every young Skyborne on Zephras Isle will learn to camp properly whether they like it or not, had told her that a fisherman’s skill is good for more than supper. There was a craft to it, Raan said: a Fish Bowl, a small bright thing to set beside a campfire so tired adventurers have something to look at besides each other. A happy adventurer is a strong adventurer. Raan believes this the way other people believe in gravity.

So Parzelle stood on the end of a pale wooden pier under a curved elven lamp, cast into the turquoise water, and waited. The lake is one of the calm places left on an island whose winds have gone wrong. The chronicler suspects she knew that and took her time on purpose. Somewhere in that hour a Longjaw Mud Snapper made the mistake of its life.

When her hands were steady enough on the rod, Fenn Fairweather at Fairweather Fishing taught her the Fish Bowl, along with the usual caution: nobody wants a camp in the middle of town, and no camp is complete without a fire. Parzelle had learned that fire last time. Mining, the other lesson in Raan’s long syllabus, she set down unfinished. A mage does not owe the earth her elbows.

Zerril Softbreeze wanted eggs and strider meat. With the cult out in the highlands nobody in Shen’dar Village has time to hunt, and Zerril, who believes nothing is wrong that a pipe of dried peacebloom and a full belly can’t fix, was running short of both. Parzelle went out into the Shen’dar Highlands and came back with enough. Zerril declared the eggs delicious fried in ursera tallow and pressed one of the famous house recipes on her, a Skywall Souffle, as if a souffle were a reasonable thing to hand a mage before sending her to a battlefield.

Out in the highlands, between the eggs and the striders, the strength settled into her again, that quiet thickening of the bones that comes from surviving things that would rather you didn’t. One more rung. Then Aonda’s errand and the tower to the southwest, which is where this account began.

One hundred fourteen minutes. Fourteen silver and change earned, not a copper spent, which may be a first for a mage. Three errands finished, one lesson abandoned, a recipe she has not yet tried, and Havoc in the Highlands, Stolen Supplies and Camping 101: Tailoring still waiting at the bottom of her satchel like debts.

The peacekeeper’s note is in her hand now. The tower door is open. The chronicler has read enough last requests to know they are rarely small, and that the people who write them almost never get to see whether anyone listened.

item.title: A Hammer Sent to Northshire
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: The recruiters came up from the harbor in the first cold week of the season, and they set their table in the Trade District where the young men drink.
item.content:encoded:
The recruiters came up from the harbor in the first cold week of the season, and they set their table in the Trade District where the young men drink.

Theramore wanted soldiers. That was the whole of the pitch, and it was a good one. Off the coast of Dustwallow Marsh, past Lady Proudmoore’s city, there is a scatter of islands the Darkspear trolls call their own, and the Theramore Expeditionary Force had decided they would look better under a blue flag. There was a muster at Northwatch Hold on the edge of the Barrens. There was pay. There was a war you could see with your own eyes, instead of the kind Stormwind fights in the House of Nobles.

Tristan Ludlowe was the first in line.

The chronicler has known a hundred young men like him, and has buried a fair number. Big through the shoulders, quick to laugh, quicker to stand up. A carter’s son from the Trade District who grew up on the stories every child in that city grows up on: the Dark Portal, the burning of the old city, the long rebuilding. His older brother Garret went to Northwatch two springs ago. The letters came often at first and then not at all, and nobody from Theramore has bothered to explain the silence. Tristan does not say he means to find out. He doesn’t have to. He signs everything the way he swings a hammer: all at once, from the hip.

The sergeant looked at the hammer, and then at him, and told him no.

Not no forever. No for now. The Expeditionary Force had enough boys who could swing a hammer. What it lacked was men who could stand up again after the hammer swung back: men who could close a wound in the field, hold a line without breaking, put a light behind them that soldiers would follow into the surf. The Church sends its candidates to Northshire Abbey, the sergeant said. Come back with the Light in you, and I’ll put you on the first ship south myself.

So Tristan went to Northshire. He went angry, which the chronicler suspects is how most paladins begin, and he went carrying a question he could not have put into words: whether the Light was something a man could use to get what he wanted, or whether it was going to want something from him first.

Northshire Valley does not care about any of that. It is the same valley it always is, gold grass and stone walls and the abbey’s windows catching the morning, and it immediately gave him chores.

Deputy Willem sent him to Marshal McBride. Marshal McBride sent him after the kobold vermin in the valley’s north end, the same sad little diggers every recruit to this abbey has been sent to thin since there was an abbey. Eagan Peltskinner, who stands by the barrels behind the building as if he were born there, wanted wolf meat from the woods past the border. Tristan brought it all back and was paid in wolfskin bracers and the faint, satisfying sense of a very small world set slightly more right.

One of the kobolds dropped a book. It had been chewed. Brother Paxton, the abbey’s librarian, received it the way a mother receives a child who has run off into the woods, and then explained, with growing distress, that the kobolds had been tunneling under the abbey and carrying off his whole collection. They must want to eat them. He sent Tristan to his assistant Daniel to count the damage. Daniel had warned Brother Paxton three times about the tunneling. Daniel also wanted very much to talk about tradeskills, and the chronicler reports, with no surprise at all, that Tristan walked out of that conversation having signed up to learn mining and herb gathering both. The boy signs things.

Then the letter. Every paladin candidate who comes to Northshire carries a Consecrated Letter to the abbey’s trainer, and Tristan carried his. What he learned in return was not a strike. It was an aura: Devotion, the steady warmth a paladin carries with him so that the men beside him stand a little harder. The chronicler finds it fitting. The sergeant had asked for exactly that, and Tristan had not understood him.

Seventeen minutes that first afternoon. The strength came twice, the way it comes to young men in the first days, quick and golden and a little embarrassing. A silver and a half earned, a good part of it handed straight to the trainer, which is the way it starts for everyone.

He came back that night for a short while and found the valley the same as he had left it. Just before he turned in, three strangers fell in beside him, one after another, the way a company forms when nobody has quite decided who is in charge.

Deputy Willem wants red bandanas taken off the Defias in the vineyards. Marshal McBride wants someone to look into Echo Ridge Mine. Brother Paxton still wants his books. Far to the south, past Theramore, the Darkspear Islands are waiting for men who can hold a line.

Tristan has not decided yet which of those fights is his. The chronicler suspects he will try to take all of them.

item.title: Copper, Greed and Giant Eggs: A WoW Forever Gold Roundup
item.dc:creator: Tim Apple
item.description: Six days into WoW Forever, my net worth is roughly one stack of linen and a strong opinion about auction deposits. I’m not alone. One player on X is level 38 with 35 gold and a 100-gold mount waiting at 40. Another asked a chatbot where to farm because they had 29 copper.
item.content:encoded:
Six days into WoW Forever, my net worth is roughly one stack of linen and a strong opinion about auction deposits. I’m not alone. One player on X is level 38 with 35 gold and a 100-gold mount waiting at 40. Another asked a chatbot where to farm because they had 29 copper.

So I did what I always do instead of farming: I read everything. Wowhead, Icy Veins, the Blizzard forums, Reddit, X, Bluesky, YouTube and a pile of guide sites. This post pulls it all into one plan.

To be clear: none of this is my idea. It’s a roundup. Every tip links to the person or site that came up with it, and the full source list is at the bottom. Where sources disagree or are guessing, I say so. Prices are from launch week and will be wrong by the time you read this. That’s how markets work, and it’s also how I work.

First, the bills

There’s no WoW Token in Forever, as Icy Veins points out, so every coin is one somebody earned. Here’s what you’re saving for:

BillCostWhenSource
Class training, 1–60206–207g, every classSpread across levelingBlizzard, Nov 2 dev notes
Apprentice Riding (first racial mount free)100g, or 90g at HonoredLevel 40Icy Veins
Dual spec50g, at any class trainerLevel 40Icy Veins
Journeyman Riding1,000g (reported by beta players, not official)Level 60WoW Forever Builds

So level 40 costs about 150 gold if you want both the mount and dual spec. Icy Veins’ advice is to buy the mount first and let dual spec wait. Paladins and Warlocks still get their mounts from class quests, per WoW Forever Builds, which is the closest thing to divine favor this economy offers.

One more change: quests at level 60 no longer turn their XP into bonus gold. Jokerd says a developer told him it’s an intentional change, possibly with a weekly gold quest added instead. Blizzard hadn’t commented officially when Wowhead wrote it up. The community is split. Some players say it goes against the “explore the world” pitch. Others think more open-world farming makes bots easier to spot. Either way, don’t save your quests for 60.

Phase 1: Leveling (1–40)

The consensus is boring, which is probably why it works: make money from the route you’re already running.

  • Don’t overspend at the trainer. Every class trains something every two levels, and you don’t need all of it. Icy Veins says skip the spells you won’t use while leveling, and put off crafting professions until later. Gathering professions are the exception.
  • Take a gathering profession, or two. Herbalism, Mining and Skinning cost almost nothing to start. Conquest Capped found that from the 30s on, a gathering profession often out-earns the mobs.
  • Check before you list. Icy Veins warns that a lot of items are selling for vendor price. Sometimes the vendor wins.
  • Fill Waylaid Crates. You get these from world drops and chests, and you can trade them, so they show up on the AH too. Fill one with a single listed material (10 Earthroot fills an Apprentice Herbs crate) and hand it in to Marcy Baker in Three Corners, Redridge (Alliance) or Dokimi by the Crossroads (Horde). You get Merchant’s Favor and reputation, and your first crate starts a one-time quest worth 50 Favor. Favor buys profession recipes. Full crate tables at Method.
  • Make a bank alt with Enchanting. Park it by the mailbox next to the AH in Orgrimmar or Stormwind and mail it every green and blue you don’t need. Install Auctionator and Disenchantry to see whether each item is worth more sold or disenchanted. Icy Veins admits this is “copper at this point, let’s be honest”, but it adds up.
  • Keep the weird greys for the Darkmoon Faire. The first Faire is up near Goldshire through Monday, Nov 16. You trade in leveling junk like Torn Bear Pelts and Soft Bushy Tails for tickets, and 50 tickets buy a 14-slot Darkmoon Storage Box from level 6. The box isn’t soulbound, so you can also sell it. Horde gets a Faire at Thunder Bluff on December 7. (That’s one well-shared post on X; I haven’t checked it in game.)
  • Fish open water. Before Fishing 205, open water in Westfall, Silverpine Forest and the Barrens brings up Tightly Sealed Trunks in about 3–8% of casts, according to Conquest Capped. Fish pools don’t drop them.
  • Don’t build your week around hyper-spawns. Blizzard sped up low-level respawns for launch and said it will turn the lower-level zones back down “once the initial launch surge of low-level characters has settled down”. The fast Dustwallow murlocs and Dun Morogh troggs have already been slowed.

Also, Blizzard patches vendor loops fast. Ceedsy’s beta video “How to get 10 gold in your first day” now opens with a note that wands sell for 1 copper. That’s the Forever economy in one sentence: someone finds a shortcut, a quarter of a million people watch it, and the shortcut gets patched.

Phase 2: Professions

  • Sell raw materials first, craft later. Icy Veins says hold off on crafting before 40, since new trainer recipes cost real silver.
  • Know your price ceiling. Mister Graphed, a Black Market vendor at Powderfuse Port in the Riverglades, sells Black Lotus, Arcane Crystal and some new Forever materials in unlimited amounts. Wowhead reads that as a price cap. So nobody is getting rich hoarding Lotus this time. Conquest Capped agrees it caps what those reagents can sell for.
  • Hunters shoot money. Two days in, one player’s AH analysis found that 10 ammo items made up 15.4% of all units sold. That’s one person’s dataset, but it’s a strong hint for Engineers and Leatherworkers (see Hunter below).
  • Mid-level herbs and ore were the strong sellers on Nov 9. Prices on the EU AH, from Conquest Capped’s scan:
MaterialSkillPrice each, EU, Nov 9
SungrassHerbalism 23037s 79c
Truesilver OreMining 23019s 95c
WintersbiteHerbalism 19518s 99c
FirebloomHerbalism 20515s 86c
Gold OreMining 1558s 58c

These will move. If you’re reading this in December, treat it as history.

Phase 3: The Auction House

The deposit. Right now every listing costs at least 1 silver in deposit. Kris Zierhut told the streamer Crix it’s going back to 1 copper: “That’s coming. Not yet, but coming.” No date yet. Once it’s live, Wowhead expects the old formula to return: 5% of vendor price for a 2-hour listing, 20% for 8 hours and 60% for 24 hours. Players had flagged the 1-silver floor as a bug back in the beta. Comment sections everywhere had feelings about that.

Until it changes:

  • List full stacks, and vendor anything that sells for about its vendor price. That’s Icy Veins’ workaround. You can also hold cheap materials until the fix lands.
  • You lose the deposit if your auction expires or you cancel it. Wowhead says so, and that matches the classic rules. One Icy Veins article says you get it back on cancel or expiry. The sources disagree, and I’d plan on losing it.
  • Sell slowly when supply is thin. Only about 240 Giant Eggs were listed on Nov 9. Conquest Capped’s advice: sell 20 at a time, not 200.
  • Check prices before you farm. One Bluesky player calls Auctionator the most vital Forever addon. Their scan found only about 7,000 things on their AH, and a profit margin of “like 50 copper.” Glamorous.
  • Prices feel high because nobody has money. Another Bluesky player points out that everyone is paying for class and profession training, and most gold still comes from quests and vendors. That’s a good reason for some patience with sellers, and with yourself.

Watch out for rollbacks. After the server restarts and emergency maintenance of Nov 8–10, players on the Blizzard forums reported that their newly trained skills rolled back but the gold they paid stayed gone. One player bought the skills again and got rolled back a second time. If the servers look shaky, maybe don’t do your big spending right then.

Farming spots by level

The 30–45 numbers come from Conquest Capped, which checked mob drops on Wowhead and priced them against the EU AH on Nov 9. Value per kill doesn’t include coin, greys or skinning.

LevelWhereWhatValue per kill (EU, Nov 9)
34–35Thousand Needles: Sparkleshell SnappersTurtle Meat, shell fragments~6s
38–39Arathi Highlands: elemental exilesCharms Warriors need for the Whirlwind Axe quest, plus elementals11–17s
39–43Dustwallow Marsh: Mudrock turtlesTurtle Meat, shells, clams~10s
40–47Feralas and Tanaris ogresMageweave Cloth~8s
41–45Tanaris: Rocs and Fire RocsGiant Eggs, Buzzard Wings~24s
42–47The Hinterlands: owlbeastsGiant Eggs (about half drop one)~38s

The Hinterlands owlbeasts are the top pick. At about 100 kills an hour, Conquest Capped puts them at 35–40 gold an hour from loot alone. The Hinterlands are contested, though, so on a PvP ruleset the Tanaris rocs near neutral Gadgetzan are the safer egg farm. Also from Conquest Capped:

  • Blue Pearls: the Giant Clams along the Stranglethorn coast hold a Blue Pearl almost every time, and the Badlands quest Pearl Diving wants nine. Black Pearls from Big-mouth Clams are a 4% lottery. Open the clams you get anyway, but don’t farm for them.
  • Fancy greys: Long Soft Tails from Swamp of Sorrows cats and Soft Bushy Tails from Badlands coyotes sell for more than normal grey items.
  • What stopped working: the Scarlet Monastery chest farm was hotfixed in the beta, Mage AoE is weaker, and turning cloth into bandages to resell no longer pays.

Level 60: it’s too early to say much. The first players only hit 60 on Nov 7. Warcraft Maps lists the usual Classic level-60 farms, like Dire Maul East and Maraudon, but labels them Classic know-how that nobody has proven in Forever yet. Treat every level-60 gold-per-hour number you see as a hope.

Class by class

The best class-by-class breakdown I found is Warcraft Maps. It’s careful to label what’s been tested in Forever and what’s just carried over from Classic. Most of this section comes from there.

Mage

  • The AoE nerfs target gold farmers by name. Blizzard’s beta notes, quoted on the forums, cut Improved Blizzard’s slow to 40% from 65% “to reduce the power of Frost Mages to AoE farm instances, which was widely used by gold farmers.” Cone of Cold got shorter, and Arcane Concentration procs less from low ranks. Warcraft Maps’ fix is to start with packs of three or four and add more as you learn.
  • Sell water, food and mana gems for tips at dungeon entrances and in capitals. Mana gems start at 28. Conjured items vanish after 15 minutes offline, so you can’t stock up overnight. Tips are voluntary, and a crowd of Mages drives them to zero (Warcraft Maps).
  • Portals: Stormwind, Ironforge, Orgrimmar and Undercity at 40, and Darnassus and Thunder Bluff at 50. The client lists a 10-second cast and a 60-second cooldown, so you can serve one group a minute.
  • Dungeon claims: one creator says solo Zul’Farrak as a 40+ Mage makes “around 40–50 gold per hour”. That’s his number, not a measured one. Morphus TV has a Revelation-plus-Blizzard trick if you’d like to test it before the next hotfix does.

Rogue

  • Pick pockets as a habit. Pick every humanoid’s pocket before you open from stealth. It’s a bonus on top of quest money, not a farm. Warcraft Maps notes that junkbox drops in Forever are still unconfirmed.
  • Open boxes for tips near the AH, using the trade window. Blacksmith keys compete with you, so tips stay modest.
  • Craft poisons. Only Rogues can make them, and only Rogues buy them. That’s a small but protected market.
  • Graveyard chests: a Forever beta video reaches both Scarlet Monastery Graveyard chests with Advanced Target Dummies (Engineering 185), Sprint, Vanish and Preparation. That’s one creator’s run, so treat it as unproven.

Hunter

  • Skin while your pet tanks. Forever adds Scarce skins like Pristine Leather, but each creature can only be skinned once, and nobody agrees on the drop rate yet.
  • Craft ammo, quivers and ammo pouches. You’re your own first customer, and the ammo sales numbers suggest plenty of other buyers. Don’t count on vendors, since Blizzard cut vendor prices on many crafted items.
  • Mind the Forever changes: Tame Beast no longer works on beasts above your level (Blizzard notes), and Warcraft Maps says traps now work in combat and Auto Shot needs you to stand still briefly. Old Classic solo routes may not work the same way.

Warlock

  • Level Affliction and keep every cloth drop. DoTs and a Voidwalker mean less drinking and more looting (Warcraft Maps).
  • Sell summons at busy dungeons. Ritual of Summoning comes at level 20 and needs two other party members to click. Meeting Stones can’t summon in Forever, which makes you more useful. Healthstones also vanish 15 minutes after logout, so hand them out as a perk rather than stock.
  • Craft Soul Bags from 40. Only Warlocks can use them, so other Warlocks are your market.

Druid

  • Travel Form herb loops from 30. You get 40% speed long before most people can afford a mount, and you can drop into Prowl to reach nodes next to camps. Warcraft Maps hadn’t seen a node picked in Travel Form yet, so test it before you plan a route around it.
  • Tauren Cultivation: grow a second copy of a herb and pick it without Herbalism. It has a 15-minute cooldown, and you need character level of at least the herb’s skill divided by 5. A Tauren Druid with Herbalism gets two herbs per stop.
  • Bear tank in pickup groups. Tanks are scarce, and scarce gets invited.

Paladin, Priest, Shaman and Warrior

  • Paladin: Consecration now only hits the first four enemies hard, so stick to small packs. The free class mount quest can save you the 100g riding bill, according to Conquest Capped (Warcraft Maps, WoW Forever Builds).
  • Priest: you earn by being useful. Heal dungeons for the drops, disenchant greens, and fill Waylaid Crates with cloth and dust (Warcraft Maps).
  • Shaman: Warcraft Maps admits it’s “not the class most players name for gold”. Use Ghost Wolf for gathering and heal to get groups. Tauren get Cultivation and Dwarves get Find Treasure.
  • Warrior: no portals, no pet, no stealth. You get a body that can stand in a pack and a seat in every dungeon group that needs a tank. Mining plus Blacksmithing turns your gear needs into a business.

What to avoid

Buying gold. Blizzard’s position is “crystal clear”: anyone found generating, selling, buying or receiving illicit gold risks losing the gold, a suspension or a permanent closure. During the beta alone, it closed more than 2,100 gold-buying accounts and almost 1,600 selling or botting accounts. Suspicious accounts can also get a Temporary Economy Hold that locks trade, mail, guild banks and the AH while Blizzard investigates. Be careful taking gold from strangers too, since receiving it counts. Report bots when you see them. Some of the “guides” you’ll find while searching are on sites that also sell gold, which tells you how seriously to take their warnings.

Need-rolling BoEs you won’t use. A hot take on X calls rolling Need on every BoE “financial responsibility”. It got 157 replies, and I’m guessing they weren’t all thank-yous. I’ll say this as gently as I can: a 5-gold weapon isn’t worth becoming the guy everyone remembers. Honest dealing pays better over time. People invite you back.

Paying for the secret. Plenty of the YouTube gold videos I checked have a paid gold guide or membership link at the top of the description, for example Solheim Gaming and Studen Albatroz. Some of those videos are genuinely useful. Just notice that one of the most reliable gold farms in WoW is selling gold guides. For a calmer free option, WoW Forever Tavern’s casual guide walks through getting the mount and dual spec at 40 without a dedicated farm.

Giving it all away to people who don’t need it. One Bluesky user wondered why people play Forever just to donate gold to streamers. Generosity is great. Maybe aim it at the level 12 who can’t afford his spells.

The point of all this

Gold in Forever is supposed to feel scarce, and right now it does. It’s easy to let that turn every evening into spreadsheets and suspicion. I’d rather not.

’Abdu’l-Bahá wrote that “wealth is most commendable, provided the entire population is wealthy” (The Secret of Divine Civilization). In Azeroth terms: get your mount, sure. But tip the Mage who saved you the boat ride. Sell your Giant Eggs a few at a time instead of crashing the market for everyone. Mail a spare bag to someone who’s still carrying everything in a backpack. Moderation works in the game too. Farm enough to fund the fun, then go have some.
